questions.q: What three questions help you find your Hedgehog concept?
a: What you can be best at, what you love and what drives economics
What you sell, who buys it and what it costs
What rivals do, what customers want and what is new
What you own, what you owe and what you earn
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the concept sits where best-in-world skill, passion and the key economic indicator meet.

questions.q: What does the hedgehog represent in Collins's analogy?
a: One simple strategy applied consistently
Speed and agility against larger rivals
Many small bets spread across markets
Careful imitation of the market leader
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the hedgehog always uses the same simple defense and comes out on top.

questions.q: When should a company adopt a new technology, according to the summary?
a: Only when it speeds progress toward the core goal
As soon as a competitor adopts it
Whenever it is cheap enough to test
Before the market has fully matured
questions.why: Lesson 2 says to jump on new tools only once they clearly help your Hedgehog concept.

questions.q: What did Walgreens do differently with e-commerce?
a: It moved carefully and used online tools to support stores
It ignored the internet until rivals disappeared
It rebuilt itself as an online-only pharmacy
It sold its stores to fund a website
questions.why: Lesson 2 says Walgreens mapped out an online strategy that boosted its pharmacy business.

questions.q: What does realistic optimism mean in this summary?
a: Face hard facts without losing faith you can solve them
Expect the best and ignore bad news
Prepare for the worst and avoid risk
Stay positive by avoiding hard conversations
questions.why: Lesson 3 says great companies neither bury their heads nor give in to despair.
